newsitem.title: USA: Clinton pledges careful study of tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton pledges careful study of tobacco deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton pledged on Sunday to study carefully a $368.5 billion tobacco settlement that some public health interest groups have criticised.

At a news conference after the Group of Seven summit in Denver, Clinton said the federal government wanted to make sure that the elements of the deal that made tobacco executives conclude it was in their interest to reach a settlement do not undermine public health.
Tobacco companies agreed on Friday to pay $368.5 billion, admit that tobacco is addictive and accept extensive federal regulation over their products and advertising.
In return, the companies would receive immunity from any further punitive liability for deception, fraud or conspiracy that might have occurred in the past.
"We're going to read it carefully against what the tobacco companies have already admitted about the addictive qualities of nicotine," Clinton said.

Some critics of the deal have questioned whether the tobacco companies should be given protection from past punitive damages and pointed out the industry has found loopholes in the past attempts to regulate it.
"I'm going to do my best to see that this whole endeavour, which is massive, results in something positive for the American people," Clinton said.
When the deal was announced, Clinton appointed an advisory panel to study it for 30 days to study all aspects of the historic agreement and weigh its potential impact.

Clinton, asked if the G7 should take up regulation of tobacco, said the United States' partners in the group -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan -- were not the primary places where the tobacco market was growing.

But he said other countries should take a look at how America was confronting tobacco and "ask themselves whether they should take similar steps if they want to avoid very high death rates, very high disease rates, and enormous social costs."
